lignes.texte: Right now, Big Tech is burning billions of dollars on machines they can’t plug in.
Silicon Valley promised AI would usher in the next industrial revolution,
sparking a bitter and relentless race to succeed. But they forgot one thing…
The power grid is maxed out. Now, state of the art data centers,
full of next gen chips, are sitting in the dark. Big Tech tried to build the future…
but built a multi-billion dollar graveyard. Ashburn, Virginia is ground zero for the AI
crisis. Nearly 50 million square feet (4.65 million square meters) of data center space
is crammed into this single county. Over 70% of the world’s internet traffic flows through here
every day. To anyone passing by, they look like thriving hubs, a testament to the digital age.
But inside, they’re hollow monuments. AI companies are being held hostage
by one local power company, Dominion Energy, who recently dropped a bombshell.
The grid is paralyzed. In 2022, the wait time to get a new data center online was 4 years.
By 2026, it had stretched to 7. Now, tech giants like Microsoft are being quoted
up to 12 years just to evaluate a connection request. Not to lay down the copper or build a
substation. Just to decide if it is even possible. Dominion’s grid has a 25 gigawatt ceiling, enough
to power millions of homes across the region. The data centers waiting in line are demanding 40
gigawatts. That’s the same output as 30 nuclear reactors, all for a small corner of Virginia.
But the blackout isn’t contained to this one part of America.
It’s spreading like a virus. Across the country, $130 billion
of real estate is sitting in limbo. And it’s causing a financial blackhole.
Nvidia rolls out a new chip every 18 to 24 months. Each new generation makes the last one obsolete,
slashing its resale value in half. By the end of the decade, a $30,000 chip bought in 2024 will be
worth the same as a used car engine block. And data centers are full of them.
Billions of dollars of silicon are sitting on pallets in a dark warehouse, slowly bleeding
value, waiting for a substation that isn’t coming. Every CEO in Silicon Valley already knows this.
But they’re ordering more chips anyway because if one of them blinks, their rivals race ahead.
If Amazon stops buying chips and Google’s dark buildings light up the next day,
Amazon never catches up. It’s a Mexican standoff, and each of these companies is terrified.
And America is caught in the crossfire.
Mark Zuckerberg has proved he’d rather burn billions of dollars
than come second in the AI arms race. He pushed Meta’s spending for 2026 to $145 billion
and it sent shockwaves through Wall Street. Investors couldn’t see how Meta would ever earn
that money back, so they immediately dumped their stock. $175 billion was wiped out in a single day.
Zuckerberg didn’t even blink.
Just 3 weeks later, he slashed 8,000 jobs… all to keep the spending alive.
Over at Microsoft, CEO Satya Nadella is gambling even bigger. In a single quarter,
Microsoft poured a record $37.5 billion into AI and data centers. That’s more than $400 million
every day. As finance chief, Amy Hood, warned that AI demand is rapidly outpacing supply, investors
turned their backs. By the end of the next day, $357 billion in value had been wiped out.
Nadella has even admitted that Microsoft has chips sitting in storage with nowhere to plug them in.
But it hasn’t stopped him from buying up more land.
Microsoft has signed $329 billion in leases for data centers that haven’t even opened.
Some of them are locked in for 20 years. And if the AI boom goes bust tomorrow,
Microsoft still has to pay every cent.
And those billions are all riding on one vital piece of hardware.
A large power transformer.
These electrical monoliths can weigh as much as an empty Boeing 747 and nobody can build
them fast enough. If Elon Musk or Zuckerberg orders one today, it won’t arrive for another
2 and a half years. By the time a building goes live, every chip inside is obsolete.
Transformer prices have skyrocketed 77% since 2019. Utilities pay it anyway, yet
America is still short 3 out of every 10 it needs. Skilled crews have to build them one at a time,
around a core of specialized steel. And only one place in the entire country can make that steel.
Butler, Pennsylvania.
The multi-million dollar AI industry is leaning its full weight on a town of 13,000.
And the town’s mill has become a focal point for the entire AI boom. And they're doing it on their
own. Transformer makers aren’t convinced the AI demand will last. Not one of them wants to get
stuck with a massive factory and no orders. Even the companies supplying the boom don’t trust it.
So America turned elsewhere.
Today, 80% of the country’s biggest transformers are imported.
Countries all over the world are fighting for the same hardware.
The richest companies on Earth are going head to head with entire governments.
And there’s no cutting in line.
It doesn’t matter if you’re Amazon or Google. The billion-dollar data
center in Ashburn is on the exact same waiting list as the local substation.
It’s a trillion-dollar industry, stuck behind a blown neighborhood fuze.
It’s a problem Big Tech can’t buy their way out of.
But while companies like Microsoft and Meta take all the risk, one company takes all the cash.
Jensen Huang, the CEO of Nvidia, is the ultimate arms dealer in this Mexican standoff.
He gets paid the moment the shipping crates leave his warehouse.
A single rack of Nvidia’s latest chips pulls as much power as about 100 American homes.
Whether the grid survives is somebody else’s problem.
Now, one state is being pushed to breaking point.
Energy demand is exploding in Texas. AI projects currently waiting to be plugged in are demanding
a massive 474 gigawatts. That’s more than 5 times the record peak of the entire Texas grid,
and data centers make up almost all of those requests.
The crisis has become so urgent that in August 2026,
Texas Governor Greg Abbott, ordered an emergency freeze on new data centers.
According to him, AI’s unquenchable thirst for power could threaten the entire state.
ERCOT, the group responsible for keeping the lights on in Texas,
issued a stark warning. They said that without a full grid overhaul, the Permian Basin,
America’s biggest oil field, could face rolling blackouts just to keep up with AI demands.
Desperate to survive, AI companies are trying to find a workaround.
They’re trying to skip the grid altogether by building their own gas plants on site.
Each of those plants needs a giant gas turbine, and GE Vernova, America’s biggest turbine maker,
decides who gets one. And they have a waiting list all the way through to 2030.
Now the tech giants are scrambling for scraps.
Every turbine they manage to secure, leaves Texas more exposed to the next blackout.
Taxpayers had put up billions to build new power plants
to act as a safety net for the public grid. Instead, 8 of the state’s chosen
energy projects have walked away after being ruthlessly squeezed out by the AI industry.
Even with its own power plant, a data center stays dark until electricians wire it in.
And that’s the one thing that can’t be ordered from a factory.
America is facing a catastrophic trade shortage. Almost 20,000 electricians leave the industry
every year. And out of the ones who stay, 3 in 10 are over 50. It’s an industry that’s in decline.
And AI companies want the best talent, so they’re making obscene offers.
On some data center jobs, electricians can pull in up to $260,000 a year.
That means a skilled worker with a toolbelt can easily outearn a software engineer.
No local contractor can come close to matching that. In Abilene, Texas, OpenAI’s $500 billion
Stargate project pays electricians almost double what local home builders can afford.
And with 100 more data centers headed for Texas, the raid on local crews is just getting started.
These battles for resources might play out one town at a time,
but the financial fallout is felt all over.
65 million Americans get their power from PJM Interconnection. It’s the largest grid in America,
stretching across 13 states and Washington, D.C., with Ashburn wedged into its heart.
Every year, PJM runs an auction that pays power plants just to stand for any sudden surges.
And every household on the grid covers that cost through its monthly bill.
For years, the system was stable.
Then the AI companies forced their way in and began devouring every spare megawatt.
In one auction, the price shot up more than 6 times. Utilities are passing those costs
on to customers and those bills are landing in mailboxes right now. Across the region,
households are paying an estimated $25 to $30 more a month than they did in 2024,
according to the research firm SemiAnalysis.
Joseph Bowring, the independent watchdog who polices PJM’s market,
traced the new costs straight to Big Tech.
Data centers, he wrote, are the primary reason for the soaring prices. By his count, data centers
have already added $29.4 billion to customers’ costs and to him, the damage is “not reversible.”
The market is completely broken.
And everyday, families across America are paying for buildings that won’t switch on for years.
The White House has demanded that new power plants are built and brought online as soon as possible.
And they want the AI companies to pay for them. One governor threatened to pull his
entire state out of PJM if the utility company didn’t do something about the unfolding crisis.
Big Tech treated it like an empty threat.
Only one thing matters to them: keeping their stock prices high.
As Wall Street continues to pump money into the AI bubble, one man refuses to buy the hype.
Michael Burry, the legendary hedge fund manager who called the 2008 housing crash,.
Now he’s combing through the AI financial statements, line by line.
And just uncovered a billion dollar illusion.
In the summer of 2026, Nvidia began shipping its next generation chip, Vera Rubin. The moment they
left the factory, the chips sitting in warehouses across America fell a full generation behind.
But Microsoft and Google couldn’t let Wall Street see the bleeding. So, they just altered a line in
their financial filings. They extended the life of their AI servers from 4 years to 6 years.
With the stroke of a pen, they pushed billions in costs further down the road. Overnight,
operation expenses disappeared and profits artificially swelled. Meta pulled the exact
same stunt, instantly padding its profits by $2.6 billion without selling a single extra ad.
Then Amazon’s own filings exposed the scam.
It had already stretched its own servers’ lives twice, padding its profits by more than
$5 billion. But in 2025, it suddenly reversed course and cut some servers back to 5 years
and admitted the reason: artificial intelligence is making hardware obsolete
faster than expected. Coming clean and telling the truth cost Amazon about $1 billion in profit.
Michael Burry estimates that Big Tech will hide $176 billion
in costs using this trick. He calls it “one of the more common frauds of the modern era.”
Nvidia immediately fired back with a defensive 7-page memo to Wall Street analysts, desperate
to claim its chips stay useful for up to 6 years. But Burry isn’t backing down. He’s now warning
that Oracle’s profits will soon be overstated by more than a quarter, and Meta’s by about a fifth.
The deception goes even deeper.
Some of the biggest debts in the AI boom are being wiped from the books.
Take Hyperion, the giant data center Meta is building in rural Louisiana.
Mark Zuckerberg once posted its outline laid over a map of Manhattan,
covering a big chunk of the island. Meta needed $27 billion to build it.
But if Meta borrowed that $27 billion itself, its stock price would tank.
So they engineered a loophole. They let an investment firm called Blue Owl own the
majority of the project, then agreed to rent it back. The debt stays off Meta’s balance sheet,
hidden from investors, while Wall Street unloads the risky bonds onto public pension funds.
Across the biggest spenders, Burry counts upward of $3 trillion in promises like this,
more than Canada’s entire economy produces in a year.
And the borrowing they can’t hide is exploding.
The industry giants are burning through cash so fast, lenders are demanding over
7% interest just to hand it over. If the giants are straining, the AI upstarts are
running dry. But Nvidia and Jenson Huang have a plan to keep chip orders flowing.
They’re bankrolling their own customers.
Nvidia has already sunk $30 billion into OpenAI and guaranteed up to $105 billion of the company’s
data center leases. If OpenAI defaults, Nvidia pays every cent. And Huang is making those
promises to a company that’s hemorrhaging money, losing $3 for every dollar it brought in in 2025.
Nvidia also owns a $4.7 billion stake in chip rental company CoreWeave. Nvidia sells
the chips to CoreWeave, and whatever computing power CoreWeave can’t sell, Nvidia buys back.
Jenson Huang is sitting on both sides of the table.
Nvidia now has well over $100 billion tied up in its own customers. Much of that money
circles straight back as chip orders and Wall Street counts every one as growth.
But the cracks are starting to show.
Oracle founder Larry Ellison borrowed tens of billions to build OpenAI’s data centers.
The reckless bet briefly made him the richest man alive.
Now half of Oracle’s future orders hang on a company that has never turned a profit.
The panic has already started.
Oracle and OpenAI abruptly pulled the plug on a planned expansion in Abilene,
the same Texas campus that raided local builders for electricians.
Wall Street turned on Ellison instantly.
The ratings agency S&P cut Oracle’s credit rating to one step above junk,
while banks are holding billions of toxic Oracle loans they can’t sell.
And now, millions of ordinary Americans are caught in the firing line.
And their life savings are at risk. The investment giant PIMCO scooped up
about $18 billion of Meta’s Hyperion bonds, using retirement money of millions to fund the deal.
If your pension is one of them, your future is propping up a half built data center in Louisiana.
Those bonds run until 2049. But Meta’s first lease on the building only lasts 4 years.
After that, Mark Zuckerberg can walk away, leaving ordinary Americans holding the bag.
And you don’t get a say in it.
To raise the $800 billion to fund the next set of data centers,
Wall Street went hunting for cash. And they found it in insurance funds.
Firms like Apollo and KKR bought up entire insurers,
the ones that sell the annuities retirees count on for a monthly check. Since 2017,
buyout-owned insurers have quadrupled the amount of money going into these data centers. But this
private credit market is already buckling. Defaults have hit the highest rate on record.
At Blue Owl, the firm controlling most of Hyperion, the stampede has already begun.
Investors in its tech lending fund tried to pull out almost 40% of their money,
two quarters in a row. Blue Owl shut it down and only released a small amount.
None of that has stopped Jensen Huang.
Nvidia has teamed up with Apollo,
KKR and 4 other Wall Street firms to raise more than $500 billion for its own customers.
Once again, most of that money will be drained from insurance and retirement funds.
If this sounds like unprecedented tech innovation, it’s not.
It’s history repeating itself.
In the 1840’s, Britain got swept up in “Railway Mania”. Building railway tracks soaked up about
7% of the economy, the equivalent of $2 trillion a year in today’s money.
The man taking their money was George Hudson,
dubbed the “Railway King.” At one point, Hudson controlled over a quarter of England’s rail lines
and used his seat in Parliament to make sure creditors couldn’t arrest him.
He ran his empire like a pyramid scheme. He paid shareholders fat dividends out of their
invested capital and dressed it up as profit. The payouts lasted only while fresh cash poured in.
Hudson’s scheme eventually came crashing down and railway stocks across Britain lost two-thirds of
their value. A third of the approved lines were never built. Families on modest incomes had sunk
their entire savings into railway shares and lost everything. Once he lost his seat in Parliament,
Hudson fled the country. But justice eventually caught up with him and he was imprisoned.
150 years later, Wall Street was the one on the hook.
In the late 1990s, techcom giant, WorldCom
fed Wall Street a wildly inflated story about internet growth.
The industry swallowed it whole and borrowed close to $1 trillion to tear
up highway shoulders and railroad beds and bury fiber-optic cable from coast to coast.
By some estimates, as much as 95% of it sat dark, just like the data centers in Ashburn.
Gary Winnick, founder of the undersea cable company Global Crossing,
saw the writing on the wall. Before the company imploded under $12.4 billion in debt,
he cashed out more than $700 million in stock.
His workers never had that option. In Rochester, New York, their 401k contributions came in company
stock they were banned from selling for 5 years. The collapse wiped them out. Winnick held on to
his $94 million mansion in Bel Air, while his staff recovered only a fraction of their losses.
WorldCom crashed even harder, triggering the largest bankruptcy America had ever seen.
Its executives had disguised billions in everyday costs as long-term investments,
pushing expenses into the future to prop up profits today. The exact same accounting fraud
Michael Burry is accusing the AI companies of in order to hide $176 billion in losses.
Inside WorldCom, employees watched $642 million in retirement savings shrink to
less than $19 million. A federal judge sent CEO Bernie Ebbers to prison for 25 years.
Half a million telecom workers lost their jobs. Investors lost trillions.
But dark fiber could sit in the ground for years and still carry the internet one day.
The chips rotting inside empty data centers can’t wait that long. With every new launch,
Jensen Huang wipes out billions in silicon.
WorldCom’s fraud gutted the savings of its own workers.
Big Tech’s stock is buried in the 401(k)s of 70 million Americans. It adds up to $10.8 trillion,
more than a third of the U.S. economy. Out of every $100 in a standard S&P 500 fund,
about $34 rides on just 7 tech giants, with Nvidia the heaviest of them all.
If they fall, those accounts fall with them.
On June 5th, 2026, the market got its first warning shot. In a single trading session,
chipmakers shed over $1 trillion, with Nvidia alone losing about $300 billion
in a matter of hours. Every retirement fund holding those stocks got hit.
And that was just one day.
When the dot-com bubble burst, the Nasdaq kept sliding for more than 2 years,
losing 78% of its value. It took 15 years to climb back.
But Washington is pushing workers deeper anyway. The White House has ordered
regulators to open 401ks to private credit to the private credit market.
The exact same toxic asset pool that Blue Owl slammed shut to its own investors.
These institutional investors want their money back.
And you’re being lined up to pay for it.
A new Labor Department rule would strip away your rights, making it harder for
workers to sue if those investments go bad. And the shift is already happening.
Empower, one of the largest 401k providers in America, has partnered with iApollo and PIMCO,
the firm holding billions in Hyperion bonds. More than 200 employers have already signed up.
Meanwhile, the men at the top are cashing out.
Over the summer of 2025, Amazon founder Jeff Bezos unloaded $5.7 billion in stock.
Jensen Huang has sold more than $1 billion of his Nvidia shares.
Gary Winnick made before Global Crossing imploded.
And yet, every single payday, the same automated order is executed.
Millions of ordinary workers use their hard earned cash to
automatically buy the overpriced AI stock the billionaires are selling.
The AI boom has created trillions of dollars in market value,
but underneath it sits a web of debt. So what happens when it all comes crashing down?
